hero.headline: Jupiter weekend beach dance parties to continue near sea turtle nests with new lighting rules
hero.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments following a meeting Wednesday at Jupiter police department.
hero.body:
The Town of Jupiter held a meeting Wednesday at the police department to discuss ongoing concerns about weekend beach dance parties in an area where sea turtles nest. The gathering brought together representatives from local, county, and state agencies along with staff from Loggerhead Marinelife Center. The meeting ran approximately ninety minutes, and organizers of the dance events reported afterward that the discussion was constructive. Following the session, Foreli of Happy Beach Dancing confirmed the weekly gatherings will proceed with modifications to their current setup.

The primary adjustment involves limiting the lighting at the events to minimize disruption to nesting sea turtles. Some community members had advocated for relocating the dance parties away from the nesting area during sea turtle breeding season, but organizers opted instead to implement the lighting changes. The Happy Beach Dancing group has operated at Beach Access 55 for the past three years, regularly attracting dozens to hundreds of attendees each week. The gatherings appeal to diverse groups, including families, children, and people bringing dogs to the beach. Organizers announced they plan to hold their next event at Beach Access 55 this Saturday.

Jupiter's beaches represent one of the world's most densely populated loggerhead sea turtle nesting sites. Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, explained that the area contains approximately 150 nests. Walczak noted that the presence of large crowds on the beach itself, regardless of the specific activity, can discourage nesting mother turtles from coming ashore to lay their eggs. This concern highlighted why the meeting became necessary and why the lighting modifications were considered important by conservation officials.

The Town of Jupiter issued a statement regarding the outcome of the meeting but the specific content was not detailed in available reporting. The decision to continue the beach dancing with adjusted lighting represents a compromise between allowing the popular community gatherings to persist and protecting the sensitive nesting habitat. The lighting restrictions aim to balance both concerns going forward. The group's commitment to returning this weekend indicates they view the new agreement as workable for their operations while addressing environmental protection goals.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents getting money back after $24 million settlement with former trash hauler
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie will return all $24 million from a settlement with Waste Pro to residents through property tax credits, with longtime homeowners receiving $364 and others receiving $64.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive money back after the city secured a $24 million settlement from Waste Pro, their former trash hauler. Both the city and company filed lawsuits against each other in 2021 during the pandemic. The city alleged that Waste Pro failed to meet its contractual service standards, while the company attributed the problems to labor shortages caused by the pandemic. Rather than receiving checks, residents will see credits applied directly to their property tax bills.

The settlement amounts vary depending on property ownership history. More than 57,000 properties with the same owner since 2022 will receive $364 credits each. The city determined that these residents experienced the most significant problems during Waste Pro's service failures in 2021 and 2022, including service interruptions. The remaining credits address rate increases that occurred while Waste Pro breached its contract, plus costs associated with litigation and transitioning to a new provider.

A second group of properties will receive $64 credits. This includes 24,676 properties that experienced title changes since 2022. Because the city cannot determine whether these changes resulted from trusts, marriage, divorce, or relocation, and cannot reach former owners, all properties in this category receive the smaller amount. Additionally, 13,241 new properties will also get $64 credits since these households have paid pandemic-related rate increases.

The city has created an opportunity for property owners who sold their homes and purchased another within the city during the same period. These residents may submit documentation proving continuous ownership to receive the remaining $300 credit on their next year's tax bill. A 180-day claims window will allow eligible households to apply. The city will establish the claims process after review by city staff and the legal department. Mayor Shannon Martin stated that from the beginning, he maintained the funds should benefit residents who experienced the problems in 2021 and 2022. Councilman Anthony Bonna said the city had reached the right balance, while Councilman David Pickett noted that residents suffered through the disputes and litigation. One resident, Kelly Lee, expressed that she was pleasantly surprised by the outcome and appreciated the city's thoughtful approach to the settlement distribution.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman arrested for posing as parking official in Palm Beach Worth Avenue scam
cards.body:
Palm Beach police arrested a 19-year-old West Palm Beach resident accused of impersonating a parking official and defrauding visitors on Worth Avenue. Ti'Miyah De'Asia Allen allegedly posed as an employee of ParkMobile and the Palm Beach Parking Authority while running a scheme that targeted unsuspecting drivers. The investigation began after victims reported fraudulent charges to police, revealing a calculated effort to steal credit card information from people trying to pay for parking in the upscale shopping district.

According to an arrest affidavit, Allen would approach drivers either before they paid for parking or while they were in the process of paying. She allegedly offered to let them pay approximately $1 for parking instead of the legitimate rate of $5 per hour plus a 40 cent transaction fee. To make the scheme more convincing, Allen carried what appeared to be a legitimate ParkMobile payment device and displayed a fake badge, police say. The convincing appearance of official credentials helped her gain the trust of her targets, many of whom were over 65 years old.

The consequences for victims have been substantial. In one documented case from June 5, a person approached by Allen reported discovering a fraudulent $2,500 charge on their credit card from a company called Health Aid. Police determined that Allen's illegal operation resulted in the town losing parking fee revenue that should have been legitimately collected. The affidavit explicitly noted this financial impact on municipal finances in addition to the direct harm to individual victims.

This is not Allen's first brush with law enforcement involving financial fraud. Police say she was involved in a similar scheme the previous year while working at a Wawa location on Belvedere Road. During that incident, she allegedly voided customer transactions for profit. The pattern of fraudulent behavior led authorities to bring multiple charges against Allen in connection with the Worth Avenue scheme. She faces charges including falsely impersonating an officer, organized scheme to defraud, and unlawful use of a badge or other indicia of authority. These charges reflect the premeditated nature of the operation and her deliberate use of false credentials to carry out the scam.

An additional 24,676 properties that had a title change since 2022 will receive $64 credits, as will 13,241 new properties. Residents who sold and purchased another home within the city during this period may submit documentation showing continuous ownership to receive the remaining $300 credit on the following year's tax bill through a 180-day claims window.

cards.headline: Hillsborough County moves to ban concentrated kratom extract as state emergency rule nears expiration
cards.body:
Hillsborough County Commissioners voted unanimously to direct the County Attorney's Office to draft ordinance changes targeting 7-hydroxymitragynine, a potent kratom extract that federal and state officials say poses abuse risks. The move comes as a statewide emergency rule restricting the compound approaches its June 30 expiration date. Commissioner Joshua Wostal, who introduced the measure, emphasized the proposal would focus exclusively on concentrated 7-OH products and not affect traditional kratom leaf sold at kava bars, coffee shops, or other local businesses.

The concentrated extract has drawn scrutiny from regulators due to its ability to bind to opioid receptors and produce stronger effects than natural kratom. FDA Commissioner Marty Makary has stated that 7-OH can be up to 13 times more powerful than morphine. The FDA has expressed particular concern about concentrated 7-OH being manufactured into fruit-flavored gummies, drink mixes, and other products potentially appealing to children, with such items sold online, in gas stations, convenience stores, and vape shops. Attorney General James Uthmeier issued the emergency rule last year, classifying isolated or concentrated 7-OH as a Schedule I controlled substance in Florida, making it illegal to sell, possess, or distribute. Wostal said he heard Uthmeier indicate plans to renew the rule at a Tiger Bay forum, but argued the county should not wait for state action to protect residents.

Florida lawmakers considered making the restriction permanent during the 2026 Legislative Session through SB 436, sponsored by Jacksonville Senator Clay Yarborough, but that language was removed before passage. This left the emergency rule as the primary statewide safeguard. Commissioner Donna Cameron Cepeda characterized synthetic opioids as a crisis demanding local attention, saying the county bears responsibility for preventing resident harm. Commissioner Chris Boles noted that designer drugs often do not respond to lifesaving overdose interventions like NARCAN, making it important for the county to stay ahead of emerging synthetic compounds that continue to evolve.

The commissioners' vote does not immediately establish a ban but initiates the county's process for reviewing its synthetic drug ordinance and determining whether local 7-OH restrictions are necessary. Wostal amended his motion to specifically target 7-OH sales while excluding kratom generally, clarifying he did not want to surprise local businesses during the drafting process. He expressed concern about the consequences if the state emergency rule expired without local protections in place.

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee to fund new fire rescue department launching Oct. 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter's town council approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department beginning Oct. 1, with the fee covering about 8% of the total cost.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The per-property charge will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department, with property taxes funding 84% and EMS transport fees covering the remaining 8%. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee on residents' tax bills. Finance Director Scott Reynolds highlighted the financial benefit to property owners, stating "The immediate savings for property owners, we've been talking about this for three years, starting at $25 million so right out of the gate, a $10 million savings to the residents." Some residents raised concerns about potential increases in the fee over time.

Mayor Jim Kuretski cast the lone no vote on the funding structure, citing concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Kuretski noted that single family homes are assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not. The town mailed letters explaining the fee to 30,000 homes. Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged confusion among residents, attributing it to the new non ad-valorem assessment. The town has established an online calculator to help residents see their potential savings.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach commission approves 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach
cards.teaser: The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, pushing the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years.
cards.body:
The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, extending the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years. The decision followed public debate over fairness, community benefit, and the timing of granting a lease extension seven years before the current agreement expires. City staff noted that Benny's had requested the maximum 30-year term allowed under city rules.

Owner Dylan Lipton defended the extension by highlighting the restaurant's 40-year presence in Lake Worth Beach, stating it has become part of the city's identity. Lipton noted the restaurant employs more than 100 local residents, invests $1 million annually in maintenance and improvements, and serves as a major tourism driver. However, several residents voiced concerns. Jenny Powell questioned what benefits residents would gain, while Kim Stokes raised concerns about unequal treatment compared to how the commission discussed the Beach Club. Nancy Udell warned against limiting future commissions' options. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan supported the extension, calling Benny's the city's highest-paying tenant. Commissioner Sarah Malega conducted an affordability check, spending $20 on a $16 sunrise breakfast. Commissioners Mimi May and Mayor Betty Resch emphasized the restaurant's role as a community institution and its ongoing property investment.

cards.headline: Delray Beach considers new e-bike rules after dangerous encounters on city streets
cards.teaser: Delray Beach city commissioner Juli Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding, and to require IDs and helmets for riders under 16.
cards.body:
Dangerous encounters with e-bikes and dirt bikes on Delray Beach streets have prompted city leaders to consider new regulations. Commissioner Juli Casale has witnessed the dangerous behavior firsthand, observing riders moving in and out of traffic, sometimes traveling on sidewalks while wearing masks. Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding, and to require identification and helmets for riders under 16. "The kids should not be riding over 20mph, they should be wearing helmets, they should carry identification and they should be very careful," Casale said. "I would be heartbroken if one of these kids got hurt in my city."

Fred Levy, from Highland Beach, who rides along A1A regularly, described the risks faced by cyclists. "It's really scary for us bikers, really scary. I say every day I have like an incident where my sort of life passes in front of my eyes," Levy said. Resident Kayla Genest, a frequent runner, has also noticed younger kids on e-bikes performing wheelies and tricks around the city. City staff will draft the ordinance and present it at a later meeting. Casale emphasized that the goal is to allow officers the opportunity to enforce the rules, stating that "Safety is our number one priority in Delray Beach."

cards.headline: Promise Fund to offer free mammogram screenings in Jupiter and West Palm Beach next month
cards.teaser: Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through events hosted by Promise Fund on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through events hosted by Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit focused on increasing survivorship from breast and cervical cancer. The organization will hold free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach. The first event is scheduled for July 11 from 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road in Jupiter, while the second will take place July 12 from 9 a.m. in West Palm Beach. The screenings are being offered in partnership with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services.

Appointments are required for both events. Those interested can register by calling 877-427-7664. Promise Fund serves women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties who are uninsured, underinsured or have limited access to health care. Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, said the organization is working to make screenings accessible for everyone, especially those who might otherwise go without care. Promise Fund has reached more than 145,000 women across South Florida through education and advocacy efforts, with more than 27,000 women receiving access to screenings, diagnostics and care through its programs, and 286 women diagnosed with cancer receiving assistance navigating treatment.

The decision generated public debate over fairness and timing. Resident Kim Stokes raised concerns about unequal treatment, questioning why Benny's wasn't receiving the same conditions as the Beach Club. Resident Jenny Powell questioned the timing of the extension, which comes seven years before the current lease expires in January 2033. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan led the extension's advocacy, calling Benny's the city's highest paying tenant by a mile. Commissioner Sarah Malega conducted an affordability check before voting, ordering the sunrise for $16. Mayor Betty Resch said Benny's deserves the stability of continuing there. The commission approved the 10-year extension unanimously, extending the lease through February 2043 with a 5 percent rent increase every two years.

cards.headline: Republican lawmakers tour Lake Okeechobee to discuss restoration efforts and water quality
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday, discussing ongoing and future efforts to revitalize the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss restoration efforts for the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians. Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County said the lake is central to the region's water systems, noting that nutrient issues, vegetation problems and management challenges converge there. Meg Weinberger, who represents western Palm Beach County, emphasized the importance of educating Floridians about the lake's significance. "Many Floridians really have no clue what goes on in Okeechobee and Lake Okeechobee, and it's very important," Weinberger said.

Congressman and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds participated in the tour and stressed completing long-planned restoration projects. He highlighted a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels and identified sediment removal as a key priority going forward. However, Friends of the Everglades Executive Director Eve Samples countered that investment should focus south of Lake Okeechobee instead. She noted the lake ranks among North America's most polluted and that the Southern Everglades face phosphorus pollution deadline failures this year, arguing that water storage and treatment projects south of the lake would deliver greater returns for taxpayers.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach approves $15 million Fern Street railroad crossing project to ease downtown traffic
cards.teaser: West Palm Beach commissioners approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street, a move city leaders say will significantly reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach commissioners have approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street designed to reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads. The project would construct a new at-grade railroad crossing between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, creating a direct connection between Fern Street and Clearwater Drive. The route is designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard, which drivers and city officials have identified as choke points in the downtown grid. Fern Street itself could be widened to five lanes to accommodate expected increases in traffic volume. City officials estimate the crossing would divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from the two congested corridors.

The commission approved two resolutions: Resolution 119-26, a $3 million state-funded grant agreement through the Florida Department of Transportation, and Resolution 120-26F, covering associated funding appropriations. The total estimated cost for the roadway portion is $14.8 million, with remaining funding coming from existing city budget allocations and future sources including HUD grants, mobility fees, and CRA funding. The city is currently in the preliminary design phase, with the project expected to go out to bid as a design-build contract in fall 2026. Construction is slated to begin in early 2027 with a target completion date of early 2028.

hero.headline: Promise Fund to offer free mammogram screenings in Jupiter and West Palm Beach next month
hero.teaser: Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through Promise Fund, which serves women in Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties.
hero.body:
Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit dedicated to increasing breast and cervical cancer survivorship. The organization is hosting free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach. These events are made possible through partnerships with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services.

The Jupiter screening takes place July 11 starting at 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road, while the West Palm Beach event is scheduled for July 12 beginning at 9 a.m. Both locations require advance appointments to participate. Women interested in attending can register by calling 877-427-7664. Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, emphasized the importance of these screenings. "The Promise Fund is here to make screenings accessible for everyone, especially those who might otherwise go without care," Lahoz said. She added that early detection can significantly impact treatment outcomes and quality of life. "Treatment is often easier to manage, and people are able to focus more on their health, their families, and their everyday lives," she explained.

Promise Fund serves uninsured, underinsured and underserved women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties. The nonprofit has made substantial progress in expanding access to care across South Florida. Through education and advocacy efforts, the organization has reached more than 145,000 women. Additionally, more than 27,000 women have received access to screenings, diagnostics and care through Promise Fund programs. The organization has also assisted 286 women who were diagnosed with cancer in navigating their treatment options.

Currently, Promise Fund operates four co-located screening programs across Palm Beach and Broward counties. The organization is actively seeking funding to expand this model to Martin County. These free screening events represent an important opportunity for women who lack adequate health insurance or have limited access to preventive care services. Early detection through mammography screening remains a critical tool for improving health outcomes and survival rates for breast cancer patients.

cards.headline: Weekend beach dance parties in Jupiter spark debate during sea turtle nesting season
cards.teaser: A popular weekend dance gathering at Jupiter beach access 55 has sparked debate over whether the events disrupt sea turtle nests during nesting season.
cards.body:
A popular weekend beach dance party at Jupiter beach access 55 has sparked debate over whether the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests during nesting season. For the past three years, the weekly event called "Happy Beach Dancing" has drawn dozens and sometimes hundreds of people of all ages, families, children, and dogs. Some residents are concerned the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests and have called for the dancers to relocate during nesting season rather than shut down the event entirely.

Jupiter's beaches rank among the densest nesting sites for loggerheads in the entire world, with 150 nests documented in this small area. Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said large crowds gathered on the beach can deter mama turtles from nesting. The center is not a regulatory agency and focuses on doing what is best for the turtles. Isabel Nylen, a longtime Jupiter resident who has attended the dance events, said she understands both sides of the debate. Her daughter Camila Nylen noted that Jupiter's beaches are special and residents have a responsibility to protect them. Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with the dance party organizers on Wednesday to discuss the issue. The Town of Jupiter is gathering all interested stakeholders for the conversation.

cards.headline: Researchers explain how sargassum helps and hurts Florida's sea turtles
cards.teaser: Sargassum plays a complicated role for sea turtles, providing critical habitat offshore but creating obstacles for hatchlings when it washes ashore in large amounts.
cards.body:
Sargassum presents a complicated challenge for Florida's sea turtles, despite being viewed as a nuisance by many beachgoers. When the brown seaweed floats offshore in ocean currents, it serves as critical habitat for hatchlings leaving the beach. Emily Turla, laboratory coordinator at Florida Atlantic University's Marine Science Laboratory and a Ph.D. student, explained that after hatching, young sea turtles spend their first days swimming away from shore, where floating mats of sargassum provide shelter from predators, food sources, and protection during one of the most vulnerable stages of their lives.

The problem emerges when excessive amounts of sargassum wash ashore. Large piles of seaweed become obstacles for hatchlings trying to reach the ocean, sometimes leaving them stuck in the debris. Research professor Dr. Brian LaPointe with FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute notes that the extra time hatchlings spend navigating around accumulated seaweed increases their vulnerability to predators. As sea turtle nesting season continues across South Florida, researchers say finding ways to manage excessive sargassum while preserving its ecological benefits will remain an important challenge for coastal communities.

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee to fund new fire rescue department launching Oct. 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The fee will replace the current county fire fee that appears on residents' tax bills.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to fund the town's new fire rescue department launching Oct. 1. The per-property fee will cover about 8% of the department's total cost, with property taxes funding 84% and EMS transport fees covering the remaining 8%. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee on residents' tax bills. Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the change delivers significant savings for property owners, with an immediate savings of $10 million to residents.

Mayor Jim Kuretski cast the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee, and Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged confusion has arisen because the town has not previously used a non ad-valorem assessment. Some residents expressed concern the new fee could increase over time. The town has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings.

cards.headline: Prosecutors to subpoena Tiger Woods medical records after Jupiter Island DUI arrest
cards.teaser: Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.
cards.body:
Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records following his not guilty plea to driving under the influence after his March arrest on Jupiter Island. The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County, announcing the subpoena will be issued on June 30 for records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization.

The subpoena will specifically seek any and all reports documenting statements Woods made regarding alcohol or chemical substance use, any and all drug screen results, and the name of the person who performed any testing. The filing was submitted by Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. Any objections to the subpoena must be delivered to the Assistant State Attorney within 10 days.

cards.headline: Two out of three Floridians say gas price increase of $1.01 could tank summer road trips
cards.teaser: A new survey shows two out of three Floridians say higher prices could tank their summer road trips this year as gas prices are starting to fall.
cards.body:
A new survey by RV Windshield Replacement shows two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could "tank" their summer road trips this year. Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel is off. "No. There is no way," said one driver at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach. "I mean, no one can unless you're rich," said another driver WPTV connected with.

The survey found 68% of Florida drivers agree shorter state trips might be most doable, but some say even that could be tough to pull off. One WPTV viewer said that instead of going to Orlando every two weeks, they now go like once a month, or even sometimes skip a month because of the gas price.

cards.headline: Erling Haaland scores twice in World Cup debut as Norway tops Iraq 4-1
cards.teaser: Erling Haaland scored twice and added an assist in his World Cup debut as Norway topped Iraq 4-1 in Group I play.
cards.body:
Haaland's performance helped Norway secure a strong start to their World Cup campaign. The Manchester City striker demonstrated his scoring prowess on the international stage, finding the back of the net twice while also contributing an assist in the 4-1 victory over Iraq.

The match marked Haaland's first appearance in a World Cup tournament. Norway's commanding performance in Group I sets them up well for the remainder of the group stage as they look to advance in the competition.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library summer reading challenge runs through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to Unearth a Story this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31.
hero.body:
Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. McMullen said returned logs will also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Little learners up to age 4 can take home a fun rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. In addition to the reading challenge, each branch is hosting special events from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs.

McMullen added that families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. Summertime reading programs help prevent the summer slide in student learning, according to the American Library Association. Logs can be picked up and turned in on-site. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach hosts Worlds Largest Swim Lesson on June 25
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park will join Live Like Jake and other participants worldwide for the Worlds Largest Swim Lesson on June 25, a coordinated effort to raise awareness about water safety.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach is offering multiple special events this summer for guests of all ages. Elliott Russell, director of marketing and sales, told WPTV that Adults Night returns with music, glow items, and exclusive park access for guests 21 and older. The event allows grown-ups to enjoy the slides, lazy river, and wave pool under the stars. General Manager Greg Fuller said families can also take advantage of free admission for dads on June 20-21 during Father's Day weekend.

On June 25, Rapids Water Park will join Live Like Jake and participants worldwide for the World's Largest Swim Lesson, a coordinated effort to raise awareness about water safety. The park, located at 6566 N. Military Trail in Riviera Beach, is open daily with various ticket packages. New viral treats including specialty funnel cakes are making an appearance this season.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce showcases Florida coastal habitats
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through fully live ecosystem displays. Since 1980, the facility has operated under the Smithsonian with a philosophy that distinguishes it from most public aquariums. Manager Bill Hoffman told WPTV the aquarium houses more species than many larger facilities and called it "the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast." The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef tank, which recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also encounter live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities that demonstrate intricate relationships between organisms, including a four-inch barracuda.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff supervision. According to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, visitors often encounter animals they have never seen before, making it a crowd favorite. The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station and aims to raise public awareness about ocean conservation threats. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on numerous small organisms. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The aquarium is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open year-round. More information is available at sms.si.edu and Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

hero.headline: Hillsborough County moves to ban concentrated kratom extract as state emergency rule nears expiration
hero.body:
Hillsborough County Commissioners voted unanimously to direct the County Attorney's Office to draft ordinance changes targeting 7-hydroxymitragynine, a potent kratom extract that federal and state officials say poses abuse risks. The move comes as a statewide emergency rule restricting the compound approaches its June 30 expiration date. Commissioner Joshua Wostal, who introduced the measure, emphasized the proposal would focus exclusively on concentrated 7-OH products and not affect traditional kratom leaf sold at kava bars, coffee shops, or other local businesses.

The concentrated extract has drawn scrutiny from regulators due to its ability to bind to opioid receptors and produce stronger effects than natural kratom. FDA Commissioner Marty Makary has stated that 7-OH can be up to 13 times more powerful than morphine. The FDA has expressed particular concern about concentrated 7-OH being manufactured into fruit-flavored gummies, drink mixes, and other products potentially appealing to children, with such items sold online, in gas stations, convenience stores, and vape shops. Attorney General James Uthmeier issued the emergency rule last year, classifying isolated or concentrated 7-OH as a Schedule I controlled substance in Florida, making it illegal to sell, possess, or distribute. Wostal said he heard Uthmeier indicate plans to renew the rule at a Tiger Bay forum, but argued the county should not wait for state action to protect residents.

Florida lawmakers considered making the restriction permanent during the 2026 Legislative Session through SB 436, sponsored by Jacksonville Senator Clay Yarborough, but that language was removed before passage. This left the emergency rule as the primary statewide safeguard. Commissioner Donna Cameron Cepeda characterized synthetic opioids as a crisis demanding local attention, saying the county bears responsibility for preventing resident harm. Commissioner Chris Boles noted that designer drugs often do not respond to lifesaving overdose interventions like NARCAN, making it important for the county to stay ahead of emerging synthetic compounds that continue to evolve.

The commissioners' vote does not immediately establish a ban but initiates the county's process for reviewing its synthetic drug ordinance and determining whether local 7-OH restrictions are necessary. Wostal amended his motion to specifically target 7-OH sales while excluding kratom generally, clarifying he did not want to surprise local businesses during the drafting process. He expressed concern about the consequences if the state emergency rule expired without local protections in place.

cards.headline: Florida Chamber announces Top 100 products for Coolest Thing Made in Florida competition
cards.teaser: The Florida Chamber of Commerce and FloridaCommerce unveiled 100 products competing for the title of Coolest Thing Made in Florida, with manufacturers from all 67 counties represented for the first time.
cards.body:
The Florida Chamber of Commerce and FloridaCommerce have unveiled the 100 products competing in the second annual Coolest Thing Made in Florida competition. The bracket-style competition showcases products made in Florida while highlighting an industry that employs more than 430,000 Floridians and pays an average annual wage of $86,405. This year's competition reached a milestone with manufacturers representing all 67 Florida counties, reflecting the strength and diversity of Florida's manufacturing sector. The Top 100 products range from aerospace and defense technologies to consumer goods, industrial equipment, and agricultural products.

Public voting to narrow the field to the Top 32 is underway through July 1. The surviving products will advance to a head-to-head tournament bracket culminating in the selection of the 2026 Coolest Thing Made in Florida. Florida Chamber and FloridaCommerce officials plan to visit the two finalist manufacturers during National Manufacturing Week in October before announcing the overall winner at the Florida Chamber's Future of Florida Forum and Annual Meeting on October 1. The contest aligns with the Florida Chamber Foundation's Florida 2030 Blueprint initiative, which aims to make Florida a Top 5 state for manufacturing jobs by the end of the decade. The complete list of Top 100 products is available through the competition website.

cards.headline: Hillsborough County escalates Tampa Sports Authority oversight concerns to Governor DeSantis
cards.teaser: Hillsborough County Commissioners voted unanimously to direct the county attorney to gather records tied to Tampa Sports Authority board members and prepare draft letters flagging potential ethics concerns to Governor Ron DeSantis and other officials.
cards.body:
Hillsborough County Commissioners voted unanimously to escalate ethics concerns about the Tampa Sports Authority to Gov. Ron DeSantis and other state officials. The vote directs County Attorney Julia Mandell to gather Sports Authority meeting minutes, financial disclosures, property records, and business records, then draft letters to DeSantis, the State Attorney's Office, and the Sports Authority itself. The action does not accuse any board member of wrongdoing but maintains pressure on the agency following an 11-page letter received June 10 from a citizen, later identified as a lobbyist, alleging conflicts of interest involving four Sports Authority members regarding the Tampa Bay Rays stadium deal. The citizen claims some members have undisclosed property that could increase in value if the project relocated.

County Chair Ken Hagan offered a contrasting perspective, stating the underlying issue is the Rays ballpark debate and that he does not believe board members acted improperly. He noted the Sports Authority does not vote on the Rays financial framework, with only the County Commission, City Council, and Community Redevelopment Agency board determining approval. Hagan supported the review but warned that if local officials ignore governance concerns, the Legislature could restructure the Sports Authority in ways leaving the county and city paying bills with reduced power. Commissioner Miller emphasized the county's fiduciary responsibility to taxpayers as a funding entity to ensure proper ethical standards.

cards.headline: Candidate qualifying complete for Northeast Florida legislative races ahead of August primary
cards.teaser: Voters in Nassau, Duval, and Clay counties now know who will appear on ballots this August and November following the completion of candidate qualifying for Senate and House races.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

House District 12 is now an open seat as Rep. Wyman Duggan reaches his term limit, setting up a November contest between Jacksonville City Council member Terrance Freeman and Democrat Ben Sandlin, who challenged Duggan in 2024. Freeman is the sole Republican candidate and has raised roughly $445,000 between his campaign and committee accounts. The district, which includes much of southern Duval County, continues to favor Republicans in voter registration.

In House District 13, former Senate Democratic Leader Audrey Gibson and former state House hopeful Leslie Scott Jean-Bart will face off in August to replace departing Angie Nixon. Gibson has about $15,000 on hand with donors including former state Senator Tony Hill and Adam Hollingsworth, former Chief of Staff for Rick Scott when he was Governor and John Peyton when he was Jacksonville Mayor. Write-in candidate Brice Galliard has also qualified, which means the August primary is open only to Democratic voters. In House District 14, incumbent Kimberly Daniels will face Rhian Tutson, a former Florida Highway Patrol trooper and Jacksonville Housing and Community Development Commission member. Daniels has more than $40,000 in the bank. Representative Dean Black faces no Republican challenger for renomination in House District 15 but will face former state House hopeful Lloyd Caulker and Chadd Charland, who entered as NPAs.

cards.headline: University of South Florida Board of Trustees elects Mike Griffin as new Chair
cards.teaser: The University of South Florida Board of Trustees unanimously elected Mike Griffin as Chair for a full two-year term after he assumed the post in April following Will Weatherford's resignation.
cards.body:
The University of South Florida Board of Trustees unanimously elected Mike Griffin as board Chair for a full two-year term. Griffin assumed the post in April following Will Weatherford's resignation. A student at USF, Griffin served two terms as student body president and was a student representative on the first USF Board of Trustees in 2001. He has served as a Trustee since 2021 and chaired the school's last two Presidential Search Committees, including the search that led to the installation of Moez Limayem as the university's ninth President. Griffin is Vice Chair and co-head of the Florida region for Sevills, an integrated real estate services company. He previously chaired the Greater Tampa Chamber of Commerce as its youngest leader in the organization's 140-year history. Griffin is also a member of the Florida Council of 100, chairs the Lions World Vision Board of Directors, and is a member of Seacoast Banking Corp.

The board also elected Oscar Horton as Vice Chair on Wednesday. Horton has served on the board since 2018 and is CEO of Sun State International. He serves on boards for Tampa General Hospital, Academy Prep Center of Tampa, Community Foundation Tampa Bay, and the Bank of Tampa, and previously served on the USF Foundation Board. The board recognized Weatherford for his service leading the board over the past five years. The USF Board of Trustees has 13 members, including six appointed by the Florida Governor, five by the Florida Board of Governors, the Student Government President, and the Faculty Senate President.

cards.headline: AAA projects record 4.62 million Floridians to travel during Fourth of July holiday stretch
cards.teaser: AAA Auto Club of Florida forecasts 4.62 million Florida residents will travel during the Fourth of July period from June 27 through July 5, breaking the previous state record set in 2025.
cards.body:
AAA Auto Club of Florida is projecting 4.62 million Floridians will travel during the Fourth of July stretch, which runs from June 27 through July 5. The extended travel period includes an extra day for the holiday weekend since Independence Day falls on a Saturday, with many businesses and offices giving workers off on Friday, July 3. AAA expects the majority of Florida travelers to use roadways, with 4.08 million traveling by auto despite high gas prices due to the war with Iran. Another 329,326 Florida travelers will use airlines, and an estimated 214,265 people will use other forms of transportation. This projected total would break the previous Fourth of July travel record in Florida set last year with 4.57 million residents traveling.

Debbie Haas, Vice President of Travel for AAA, said that for many families, traveling for Independence Day is a tradition and that vacations are one category where consumers are still willing to spend, even if that means cutting back elsewhere. Nationally, AAA forecasts 72.2 million Americans will travel during the Independence Day period, with about 61.4 million moving on roadways, 5.84 million taking to the skies, and 4.9 million traveling by other modes. Of those national travelers, many are heading to Florida. AAA figures using travel bookings show Orlando is the second-most popular destination in the United States, with Miami fourth and Fort Lauderdale seventh.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg relaunches voter education campaign as part of America250 celebration
cards.teaser: St. Petersburg revived its St. Pete Votes campaign to encourage voter registration and turnout ahead of the 2026 elections, folding voter participation into the city's America250 celebration.
cards.body:
Mayor Ken Welch announced that St. Petersburg is reviving its St. Pete Votes campaign, first launched in 2024, as part of the city's We Are St. Pete America250 celebration. The renewed initiative encourages voter registration and turnout ahead of the 2026 elections, which mark the 250th anniversary of the United States. "2026 marks the 250th anniversary of the United States, a solemn reminder of how far our nation has come and how many people throughout history have fought, struggled, and sacrificed to secure and protect our right to vote," Welch said. The voter education campaign will focus on helping residents understand recent changes to Florida voting laws, particularly those affecting vote-by-mail ballot requests, voter ID requirements, and election deadlines. Residents are encouraged to check their voter registration status, confirm their polling place, and review updated voting guidance.

St. Pete Votes will work with neighborhood associations, local organizations, and community leaders to distribute voter education materials and encourage civic participation. The 2026 Primary is scheduled for August 18, with a voter registration deadline of July 20. Early voting runs from August 4 through August 15. The General Election is scheduled for November 3, with a voter registration deadline of October 5. Early voting runs from October 18 through November 1. America250 programming features a July 1 ceremonial flag raising at City Hall, Independence Day programming at the St. Pete Pier with a larger-than-usual fireworks display, online reading lists through the St. Petersburg Library System, a youth poster display through Parks and Recreation, and the city's annual Veterans Day Ceremony in November.

cards.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments. The Town of Jupiter convened a meeting Wednesday afternoon to address concerns about the events held where sea turtles nest.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman allegedly posed as parking official to run $1 scam in Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Palm Beach police say a 19-year-old woman allegedly impersonated a parking official and targeted drivers with a $1 parking scam on Worth Avenue. Investigators say Ti'Miyah De'Asia Allen stole credit card info from unsuspecting visitors.
cards.body:
Palm Beach police say a 19-year-old woman allegedly impersonated a parking official and targeted drivers with a $1 parking scam. Ti'Miyah De'Asia Allen of West Palm Beach posed as a parking official with ParkMobile and the Palm Beach Parking Authority on Worth Avenue, and stole credit card information from unsuspecting visitors. According to an arrest affidavit, one person Allen approached on June 5 claimed a fraudulent transaction in the amount of $2,500 appeared on their credit card to a company called "Health Aid." Police say the scheme often involved Allen telling those looking to pay for parking that they could pay her around $1 instead of the actual $5 an hour, plus a 40 cent transaction fee.

Victims say Allen was carrying what looked like a ParkMobile payment device and a fake badge, and would approach vehicles before they paid for parking or while they were paying. Police say the people targeted were over 65 years old. The affidavit states the town was "deprived of parking fee revenue that would have otherwise been legitimately paid." Police say Allen was involved in a similar scheme last year while working at Wawa on Belvedere Road, and was alleged to have voided customer transactions for profit. cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach commission approves 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach
cards.teaser: The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, pushing the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043. The extension comes with a 5% rent increase every two years.
cards.body:
The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, extending the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years. Owner Dylan Lipton defended the extension by highlighting the restaurant's four-decade presence in the community, noting it employs more than 100 local residents, invests $1 million annually in maintenance and improvements, and serves as a major tourism driver. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan led advocacy for the extension, calling Benny's the city's highest-paying tenant "by a mile." Commissioner Sarah Malega said she conducted an affordability check before voting, ordering the sunrise for $16 before tip. Commissioner Mimi May cited the restaurant's ongoing property investment and its role as a community institution hosting weddings and celebrations. Mayor Betty Resch framed the extension as providing stability for the long-standing business.

Public comment revealed significant opposition. Resident Jenny Powell questioned the timing of extending the lease seven years before the current agreement expires and asked what residents would gain. Resident Kim Stokes raised concerns about unequal treatment, comparing the commission's approach to Benny's with recent discussions about the Beach Club. Resident Nancy Udell warned the commission against limiting future elected officials' options, stating the Lake Worth Pier is a valuable public asset and should not be subject to decisions that "tie the hands of future commissions."

cards.headline: Floridians say summer road trips could be canceled if gas prices rise by $1.01
cards.teaser: Gas prices are starting to fall just in time as a new survey shows two out of three Floridians say higher prices could tank their summer road trips this year. Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel is off.
cards.body:
A new survey by RV Windshield Replacement shows that two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could cancel their summer road trips this year. The survey found that if gas prices rise another $1.01, Florida drivers say their summer travel plans are off the table. According to the poll, 68% of Florida drivers agree that shorter state trips might be the most doable option, though some say even that could be difficult to manage.

WPTV Anchor Hollani Davis spoke with drivers at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach about whether they could afford higher prices. One driver responded, "No. There is no way." Another driver added, "I mean, no one can unless you're rich." A WPTV viewer shared how rising costs have already changed their travel habits, saying they now go to Orlando once a month instead of every two weeks, and sometimes skip months entirely because of gas prices. Gas prices are starting to fall, which could provide relief for drivers planning summer travel.

cards.headline: Delray Beach considers new e-bike rules after dangerous encounters on city streets
cards.teaser: Dangerous encounters with e-bikes and dirt bikes on Delray Beach streets have city leaders considering new rules. City commissioner Juli Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding.
cards.body:
City Commissioner Juli Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to address dangerous e-bike and dirt bike behavior on Delray Beach streets. Casale has witnessed riders moving in and out of traffic, sometimes riding on sidewalks and wearing masks. The proposed ordinance would crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding while requiring helmets and identification for riders under 16. "The kids should not be riding over 20mph, they should be wearing helmets, they should carry identification and they should be very careful," Casale said.

Residents have reported safety concerns about the e-bike activity. Fred Levy, from Highland Beach, who rides along A1A regularly, said the scenic route comes with risks. "It's really scary for us bikers, really scary. I say every day I have like an incident where my sort of life passes in front of my eyes," Levy said. Frequent runner Kayla Genest said she has seen younger kids on e-bikes around the city doing wheelies and other tricks. City staff will draft the ordinance and present it at a later meeting. Casale said the goal is to give officers the tools they need to enforce the rules, with safety as the top priority in Delray Beach.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents to receive credits from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive credits on their property tax bills after the city received a $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro. The city and company filed lawsuits against each other in 2021 during the pandemic. The city claimed Waste Pro breached its contract for standard of service, while the company blamed a pandemic labor shortage. The city council voted to return all settlement funds to residents through property tax credits rather than physical checks. Mayor Shannon Martin said the funds should benefit residents who experienced issues in 2021 and 2022, while Councilman Anthony Bonna said the city reached the sweet spot with the distribution plan.

More than 57,000 properties with the same owner since 2022 will receive $364 credits, as the city determined these residents experienced the most severe issues including service interruption. Thousands of other homes will receive $64 credits due to rate increases during Waste Pro's breach of contract, including costs for a new waste site, litigation costs and switching providers. The city said 24,676 properties had title changes since 2022 and will receive $64 credits, as the city cannot distinguish between changes from trusts, marriage, divorce or relocation. The same $64 credit applies to 13,241 new properties. Residents who sold and repurchased homes within the city during this period may submit ownership documentation to receive the remaining $300 credit on the following year's tax bill through a 180-day claims window.

cards.headline: Promise Fund to offer free mammogram screenings in Jupiter next month
cards.teaser: Women in Jupiter will have access to free mammogram screenings on July 11 through Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit focused on breast and cervical cancer survivorship.
cards.body:
Promise Fund will hold free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach. The Jupiter event is scheduled for 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road, while the West Palm Beach screening will take place July 12 from 9 a.m. The screenings are being offered in partnership with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services. Appointments are required for both events. Those interested can register by calling 877-427-7664.

Promise Fund serves women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties who are uninsured, underinsured or have limited access to health care. Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, said early detection can make a real difference, noting that treatment is often easier to manage when cancer is caught early. Promise Fund has reached more than 145,000 women across South Florida through education and advocacy efforts. More than 27,000 women have received access to screenings, diagnostics and care through its programs, and 286 women diagnosed with cancer have received assistance navigating treatment. The nonprofit currently operates 4 co-located screening programs in Palm Beach and Broward counties.

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee to fund new fire rescue department starting Oct. 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The fee will cover about 8 percent of the total cost of the department. Property taxes will fund 84 percent, with the remaining 8 percent collected through EMS transport fees. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee that appears on residents' tax bills.

Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the move represents significant savings for property owners, with immediate savings starting at $25 million and a $10 million savings to residents right out of the gate. Mayor Jim Kuretski was the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee and has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman allegedly posed as parking official in Palm Beach to steal credit card information
cards.teaser: Palm Beach police say a 19-year-old woman allegedly impersonated a parking official and targeted drivers with a $1 parking scam on Worth Avenue.
cards.body:
Palm Beach police say 19-year-old Ti'Miyah De'Asia Allen of West Palm Beach posed as a parking official with ParkMobile and the Palm Beach Parking Authority on Worth Avenue and stole credit card information from unsuspecting visitors. According to an arrest affidavit, one person Allen approached on June 5 claimed a fraudulent transaction in the amount of $2,500 appeared on their credit card to a company called "Health Aid."

Police say the scheme often involved Allen telling those looking to pay for parking that they could pay her around $1 instead of the actual $5 an hour, plus a 40 cent transaction fee. Victims say Allen was carrying what looked like a ParkMobile payment device and a fake badge and would approach vehicles before they paid for parking or while they were paying. Police say the people targeted were over 65 years old. The affidavit states the town was "deprived of parking fee revenue that would have otherwise been legitimately paid." Police say Allen was involved in a similar scheme last year while working at Wawa on Belvedere Road and was alleged to have voided customer transactions for profit. Allen has been charged with falsely impersonating an officer, organized scheme to defraud and unlawful use of a badge or other indicia of authority.
